english: it's been decided that; end up doing
use: For plans settled by others or by circumstance; the past, -koto ni natta, is the usual way to announce news.
name: decided for you
formation: dictionary form or -nai form + koto ni naru

example.romaji: raigetsu oosaka ni tenkin suru koto ni natta yo
example.ja: 来月大阪に転勤することになったよ
example.english: I'm being transferred to Osaka next month.

examplePolite.romaji: raigetsu oosaka ni tenkin suru koto ni narimashita
examplePolite.ja: 来月大阪に転勤することになりました
examplePolite.english: I'll be transferring to Osaka next month.

notes: Compare -koto ni suru, where you made the choice yourself. -koto ni natte iru states a rule or standing arrangement.

use: Usually past, -koto ni shita, to report a choice you made; -koto ni shite iru means it's your habit or rule.
name: your own decision
formation: dictionary form or -nai form + koto ni suru

example.romaji: ashita kara hashiru koto ni shita
example.ja: 明日から走ることにした
example.english: I've decided to start running tomorrow.

examplePolite.romaji: ashita kara hashiru koto ni shimashita
examplePolite.ja: 明日から走ることにしました
examplePolite.english: I've decided to start running tomorrow.

notes: Compare -koto ni naru (decided for you). To choose an item, use noun + ni suru: 'koohii ni suru'.

english: tell someone to; ask someone to
use: Reports an instruction indirectly; put the verb in -nai form for 'told not to'.
name: tell someone to
formation: dictionary form or -nai form + you ni iu (also tanomu, tsutaeru)

example.romaji: isha ni sake o yameru you ni iwareta
example.ja: 医者に酒をやめるように言われた
example.english: The doctor told me to quit drinking.

examplePolite.romaji: isha ni osake o yameru you ni iwaremashita
examplePolite.ja: 医者にお酒をやめるように言われました
examplePolite.english: My doctor told me to stop drinking.

notes: Most often passive: -you ni iwareta, 'I was told to'. To pass on a message: '-you ni tsutaete' (tell them to).

english: make a point of; try to (as a habit)
use: For an ongoing effort, not a one-off attempt; -you ni shite iru means 'I make sure to'.
name: make a point of
formation: dictionary form or -nai form + you ni suru

example.romaji: yoru wa amai mono tabenai you ni shiteru
example.ja: 夜は甘い物食べないようにしてる
example.english: I try not to eat sweets at night.

examplePolite.romaji: yoru wa amai mono o tabenai you ni shite imasu
examplePolite.ja: 夜は甘い物を食べないようにしています
examplePolite.english: I make a point of not eating sweets at night.

notes: Don't mix with -you ni naru (come to be able to) or -ou to suru (try once).

use: For a good result; the helper comes first.
name: thanks to
formation: noun + no okage de; plain-form clause + okage de

example.romaji: kimi no okage de maniatta yo
example.ja: 君のおかげで間に合ったよ
example.english: Thanks to you, I made it in time.

examplePolite.ja: 皆さんのおかげで間に合いました
examplePolite.english: Thanks to all of you, we made it in time.

notes: 'okage sama de' is the set reply to 'how are you / how did it go?': 'fine, thanks'. For a bad result use no sei de.

use: For a bad result, pinning it on the cause.
name: because of (blame)
formation: noun + no sei de; plain-form clause + sei de

example.romaji: kaze no sei de zenzen nemurenakatta
example.ja: 風邪のせいで全然眠れなかった
example.english: I couldn't sleep at all because of this cold.

examplePolite.romaji: kaze no sei de zenzen nemuremasen deshita
examplePolite.ja: 風邪のせいで全然眠れませんでした
examplePolite.english: I couldn't sleep at all because of my cold.

notes: 'X no sei da' means 'it's X's fault': 'watashi no sei?' (is it my fault?). Compare okage de for good results.

use: The person or thing blamed goes before no sei; often a complaint about unfair blame.
name: blame it on

example.romaji: nandemo hito no sei ni suru na yo
example.ja: 何でも人のせいにするなよ
example.english: Don't blame everything on other people.

examplePolite.romaji: nandemo hito no sei ni shinaide kudasai
examplePolite.ja: 何でも人のせいにしないでください
examplePolite.english: Please don't blame everything on others.

notes: 'watashi no sei ni shinaide' = don't put it on me. Pairs with no sei de, 'because of'.

use: Explains why something went wrong, usually your own slip, in a soft, apologetic way.
name: excuse 'because'
formation: plain form + mon dakara (noun or na-adjective + na mon dakara)

example.romaji: kyuu ni ame ga futte kita mon dakara, okurechatta
example.ja: 急に雨が降ってきたもんだから、遅れちゃった
example.english: It suddenly started raining, so I ended up late.

examplePolite.romaji: kyuu ni ame ga futte kita mono desu kara, okurete shimaimashita
examplePolite.ja: 急に雨が降ってきたものですから、遅れてしまいました
examplePolite.english: It suddenly started raining, so I'm afraid I was late.

notes: Also mon de: 'isogashikatta mon de'. It sounds like an excuse, so use -kara or -node for a neutral reason.

use: Stresses that this reason is the real point, often turning a seeming drawback into the reason.
name: precisely because

example.romaji: taisetsu da kara koso, hakkiri iu n da yo
example.ja: 大切だからこそ、はっきり言うんだよ
example.english: It's precisely because you matter that I'm being blunt.

examplePolite.romaji: taisetsu da kara koso, hakkiri iu n desu
examplePolite.ja: 大切だからこそ、はっきり言うんです
examplePolite.english: It's precisely because you matter to me that I'm being frank.

notes: Compare kara tte, 'just because ... doesn't mean'. Koso alone stresses the word before it: 'kochira koso' (likewise, the pleasure's mine).

use: Speech often drops the o: 'shiranai furi suru'.
name: pretend
formation: plain form + furi o suru; noun + no furi; na-adjective + na furi

example.ja: 彼女、聞こえないふりしてたよ
example.english: She was pretending not to hear.

examplePolite.romaji: kanojo wa kikoenai furi o shite imashita
examplePolite.ja: 彼女は聞こえないふりをしていました
examplePolite.english: She was pretending not to hear.

notes: Also written フリ. The everyday ones are 'shiranai furi' (playing dumb) and 'neta furi' (pretending to sleep).

use: Mostly past, -ou to shita, for an attempt that failed or got interrupted: 'I was just about to'.
name: try to / about to

example.romaji: neyou to shitara, tomodachi kara denwa ga kita
example.ja: 寝ようとしたら、友達から電話が来た
example.english: Just as I was going to sleep, a friend called.

examplePolite.romaji: neyou to shitara, tomodachi kara denwa ga kimashita
examplePolite.ja: 寝ようとしたら、友達から電話が来ました
examplePolite.english: Just as I was about to go to sleep, a friend called.

notes: Compare -te miru (try it and see) and -ou to omou (plan to). Negative: 'kikou to shinai' (won't even listen).

english: have no intention of; don't feel like
name: no intention

example.romaji: mou ano mise ni iku ki wa nai yo
example.ja: もうあの店に行く気はないよ
example.english: I've got no intention of going to that place again.

examplePolite.romaji: mou ano mise ni iku ki wa arimasen
examplePolite.ja: もうあの店に行く気はありません
examplePolite.english: I have no intention of going to that shop again.

notes: The positive is -ki ga aru (be willing): 'yaru ki aru?' (are you up for it?). 'yaru ki' alone means motivation.

english: try doing (said to a child or junior)
use: A gentle 'go on, try it' from parents, teachers or seniors.
name: go on, try it

example.ja: ちょっと食べてごらん、おいしいよ
example.english: Go on, have a taste, it's good.

notes: Never use it upward; to equals say -te mite. 'goran kudasai' is the polite 'please look' in shops and announcements.

use: The fuller, firmer version of -cha dame; heard in rules, warnings and from parents and teachers.
name: must not

example.romaji: koko de shashin totcha ikenai n da yo
example.ja: ここで写真撮っちゃいけないんだよ
example.english: You're not allowed to take photos here.

examplePolite.romaji: koko de shashin o totte wa ikemasen
examplePolite.ja: ここで写真を撮ってはいけません

notes: -nakya ikenai / -nakereba ikenai means 'must'. On its own, 'ikenai!' means 'oh no' or 'oops, that's bad'.

use: A fuller, more formal way to say the potential form; common in rules, signs and polite explanations.
name: be able to

example.romaji: kono apuri de yoyaku suru koto mo dekiru yo
example.ja: このアプリで予約することもできるよ
example.english: You can also book with this app.

examplePolite.romaji: kono apuri de yoyaku suru koto mo dekimasu
examplePolite.ja: このアプリで予約することもできます
examplePolite.english: You can also make a booking with this app.

notes: Everyday speech usually prefers the potential form (taberareru, yomeru); -koto mo dekiru, 'can also', is where it sounds most natural.

use: Reassures someone or tells them not to bother: 'you don't have to go that far'.
name: no need to

example.romaji: sonna ni ayamaru koto nai yo
example.ja: そんなに謝ることないよ
example.english: There's no need to apologize so much.

examplePolite.romaji: sonna ni ayamaru koto wa arimasen yo
examplePolite.ja: そんなに謝ることはありませんよ
examplePolite.english: There's no need to apologize like that.

notes: Speech often drops wa. Don't mix with -ta koto wa nai, 'have never'.

use: Something is possible but wrong for social or moral reasons: 'I can't just leave him there'.
name: can't very well
formation: dictionary form + wake ni wa ikanai; -nai form + wake ni wa ikanai = have to

example.romaji: kyou wa kaisha yasumu wake ni wa ikanai n da
example.ja: 今日は会社休むわけにはいかないんだ
example.english: I can't very well skip work today.

examplePolite.romaji: kyou wa kaisha o yasumu wake ni wa ikanai n desu
examplePolite.ja: 今日は会社を休むわけにはいかないんです
examplePolite.english: I really can't take today off work.

notes: After -nai it means 'have no choice but to': 'ikanai wake ni wa ikanai' (I can't not go). Don't mix with wake ja nai (it's not that).

use: A strong, principled 'should'; for friendly advice -ta hou ga ii sounds softer.
name: should
formation: dictionary form + beki (suru often becomes subeki)

example.romaji: sore wa saki ni iu beki datta yo
example.ja: それは先に言うべきだったよ
example.english: You should have said that first.

examplePolite.romaji: sore wa saki ni iu beki deshita ne
examplePolite.ja: それは先に言うべきでしたね
examplePolite.english: You should have mentioned that first.

notes: -beki datta = should have; -beki ja nai = shouldn't.
